1#1768Merge Strings AlternatelyEasy

You are given two strings, word1 and word2. Build a new string by taking letters alternately: first letter of word1, first letter of word2, second letter of word1, second of word2, and so on. If one string runs out, append all the remaining letters of the other string. Return the merged string. Example: 'abc' and 'pq' give a, p, b, q, then the leftover c → 'apbqc'.

Example input"abc", "pq"
→
Output"apbqc"

Why? 'abc' and 'pq': take a, p, b, q. Only 'c' is left, so add it → apbqc.

💡 Key idea Use one index i. Take word1[i], then word2[i], if each still exists.

Edge / failure case '','xyz' → 'xyz'
word1 is empty, so nothing alternates — the answer is just word2.

2#1071Greatest Common Divisor of StringsEasy

A string t 'divides' a string s if s is t repeated one or more times (t + t + … = s). Given two strings str1 and str2, return the longest string x that divides BOTH of them, or an empty string if there is none. Example: 'ABCABCABC' is 'ABC' three times and 'ABCABC' is 'ABC' twice, so the answer is 'ABC'.

Example input"ABCABCABC", "ABCABC"
→
Output"ABC"

Why? 'ABCABCABC' is ABC three times. 'ABCABC' is ABC two times. So ABC divides both.

💡 Key idea If str1+str2 ≠ str2+str1 there is no answer. Otherwise the answer's length is gcd(len1, len2).

Edge / failure case 'LEET','CODE' → ''
No string repeats to build both words, so the answer is the empty string.

→

→

→

Return the positions in any order. Example: s='cbaebabacd', p='abc' → 'cba' starts at 0 and 'bac' starts at 6 → [0, 6].

Example inputs="cbaebabacd", p="abc"
→
Output[0, 6]

Why? Where in the text does a rearrangement of the word p appear? 'cbaebabacd' with p='abc' → starts at 0 ('cba') and 6 ('bac').

💡 Key idea Slide a window the same length as p. Keep letter counts for the window and for p; when they match, record the start. Each step adds one letter and drops one.

Edge / failure case s="abab", p="ab" → [0, 1, 2]
Windows overlap: 'ab' at 0, 'ba' at 1 and 'ab' at 2 are all rearrangements of 'ab'.

13#751IP to CIDRMedium

An IP address like 255.0.0.7 is really a 32-bit number. A CIDR block 'a.b.c.d/x' covers a run of consecutive addresses starting at that address; its size is 2^(32 − x), and the start address must be a multiple of that size. Given a starting address ip and a count n, return the SMALLEST list of CIDR blocks that covers exactly the n addresses starting at ip — no address outside that range, none missing. Example: ip='255.0.0.7', n=10 → ['255.0.0.7/32', '255.0.0.8/29', '255.0.0.16/32'] (1 + 8 + 1 = 10 addresses).

Example inputip="255.0.0.7", n=10
→
Output["255.0.0.7/32", "255.0.0.8/29", "255.0.0.16/32"]

Why? Cover exactly n consecutive IP addresses with as few 'CIDR blocks' as possible. A block starting at an address can only be as big as that address's lowest set bit allows.

💡 Key idea Treat the IP as a 32-bit number. At each start, take the biggest block that is both aligned (lowest set bit) and not larger than what is left (n). Write it as ip/(32−log2 size).

Edge / failure case ip="0.0.0.0", n=1 → ['0.0.0.0/32']
A single address needs one block of size 1, written /32.

16#900RLE IteratorMedium

A long list of numbers is stored in run-length form: encoding = [count1, value1, count2, value2, …] means count1 copies of value1, then count2 copies of value2, and so on. Example: encoding [3,8,0,9,2,5] stands for 8,8,8,5,5. next(2) → 8, next(1) → 8, next(1) → 5, next(2) → -1 (only one 5 is left).

→
Output8, 8, 5, -1

→
Output1

💡 Key idea Each question removes one person: if the candidate knows i, the candidate cannot be the celebrity (i is the new candidate); otherwise i cannot be. After one pass check the single survivor against everyone.

Everyone knows someone, so nobody is known-by-all and knows-nobody: there is no celebrity (-1).

20#3953Maximum Score With Co-Prime ElementHard

You are given a list nums and a number maxVal. You may change any element to any positive whole number up to maxVal; each change costs 1. Two numbers are co-prime if their only common divisor is 1. After the changes, you must pick one index i whose value is co-prime with EVERY other element. The score is (the final value of nums[i]) minus (the total number of elements you changed). Output4

Edge / failure case nums [2, 4], maxVal=4 → 3
2 and 4 share a factor; the best is to keep one of them and change the other to 1.

23#460LFU CacheHard

Design a cache (a small fast memory) with a fixed capacity that evicts the Least Frequently Used key when it is full; if several keys are tied for least frequently used, evict the one that was used longest ago. get(key) returns the value or -1; put(key, value) stores a value. Both calls count as 'using' the key. Aim for constant time per call. Example (capacity 2): put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1) → 1, put(3,3) evicts key 2, get(2) → -1, get(3) → 3, put(4,4) evicts key 1, get(1) → -1, get(3) → 3, get(4) → 4.

Example inputcapacity 2: put 1, put 2, get 1, put 3, get 2, get 3, put 4, get 1, get 3, get 4
→
Output1, -1, 3, -1, 3, 4

Why? A cache with a fixed size. When full, throw out the Least Frequently Used key; if tied, the one used longest ago.

💡 Key idea Keep each key's use-count, group keys into buckets by count (each bucket remembers order), and track the smallest count. Evict from the front of the smallest bucket; a use moves a key to the next bucket.

Edge / failure case capacity 0: put(1,1), get(1) → [None, -1]
Capacity 0 means nothing can ever be stored, so get returns -1.

39#3072Distribute Elements Into Two Arrays IIHard

You are given a list nums of different numbers. Build two lists arr1 and arr2: put the first number in arr1 and the second number in arr2. For every later number x, count how many numbers already in each list are strictly GREATER than x. Put x in arr1 if arr1 has the larger count and in arr2 if arr2 has the larger count; if the counts are equal put it in the list with fewer numbers, and if the lists have the same length put it in arr1. Return arr1 followed by arr2. Example: [2,1,3,3] → [2,3,1,3].

Example input[2, 1, 3, 3]
→
Output[2, 3, 1, 3]

Why? Deal numbers into two lists: the first to list 1, the second to list 2, then each next number goes to the list in which MORE elements are greater than it (ties: the shorter list, then list 1).

💡 Key idea You need 'how many elements already in a list are greater than x' fast. Compress the values to ranks and keep a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) per list that counts values; a prefix query gives the number ≤ x.

Edge / failure case [5, 14, 3, 1, 2] → [5, 3, 1, 2, 14]
The first two numbers start the lists; then each new number goes to the list with more elements greater than it, or the shorter list on a tie.

40#3161Block Placement QueriesHard

A number line starts at 0 and extends right. You process queries in order. [1, x] places an obstacle at position x (no two obstacles share a position). [2, x, sz] asks: can a block of length sz be placed somewhere in the part from 0 to x (the block must lie completely inside [0, x] and may touch obstacles only at its ends, not cover one)? Return the answers to the type-2 queries as a list of true/false. Example: [[1,2],[2,3,3],[2,3,1],[2,2,2]] → obstacle at 2; a block of 3 does not fit in [0,3]; a block of 1 does; a block of 2 fits in [0,2] → [false, true, true].

Example input[[1,2],[2,3,3],[2,3,1],[2,2,2]]
→
Output[False, True, True]

Why? A number line gets obstacles one at a time. Between them you are asked: can a block of length sz fit somewhere in the part from 0 to x without touching an obstacle?

💡 Key idea Store for each obstacle the gap to the obstacle before it, in a segment tree for 'maximum over a range'. Adding an obstacle splits one gap into two (two point updates). A query takes the maximum gap among obstacles ≤ x, also considering the open stretch from the last obstacle to x.

Edge / failure case a single query, no obstacles → [True]
There are no obstacles at all, so a block of length 5 fits into [0, 5].

5#1797Design Authentication ManagerMedium

Design an AuthenticationManager. Every token is valid for timeToLive seconds after it is generated or renewed. generate(tokenId, t) creates a token at time t; renew(tokenId, t) extends an UNEXPIRED token to expire timeToLive seconds after t (nothing happens if it is unknown or already expired); countUnexpiredTokens(t) returns how many tokens are still valid at time t (a token that expires exactly at time t is already expired). Example (ttl 5): renew('aaa',1) → nothing; generate('aaa',2); count(6) → 1; generate('bbb',7); renew('aaa',8) → nothing (expired at 7); renew('bbb',10) → expires 15; count(15) → 0.

Example inputttl 5: renew aaa@1, generate aaa@2, count@6, generate bbb@7, renew aaa@8, renew bbb@10, count@15
→
Output1, 0

Why? Login tokens expire timeToLive seconds after they are created or renewed. Support generate, renew (only if not yet expired) and counting the unexpired tokens.

💡 Key idea Store each token's expiry time. Renew only if its expiry is still in the future; counting means counting expiries greater than the current time.

Edge / failure case renew after expiry → [None, None, 0]
The token expired at time 6, so renewing at time 10 does nothing and no token is active at 11.

Design a stack with a maximum size and one extra operation. CustomStack(maxSize) creates it; push(x) adds x on top unless the stack is full; pop() removes and returns the top (−1 if empty); increment(k, val) adds val to each of the bottom k elements (or to all if there are fewer than k). Example (maxSize 3): push 1, push 2, pop → 2, push 2, push 3, push 4 (ignored: full), increment(5,100), increment(2,100), then pops return 103, 202, 201, −1.

→

The stack holds at most 1 item, so the second push is ignored; the second pop finds it empty (-1).

You are given two binary trees (boxes called nodes with up to two children). Lay one on top of the other to merge them: wherever BOTH have a node, the merged node holds the SUM of the two values; where only one has a node, use that node. Return the merged tree. Example: [1,3,2,5] and [2,1,3,null,4,null,7] → [3,4,5,5,4,null,7]. (A tree written as a list reads level by level, top to bottom and left to right; null means there is no node in that spot.)

→
Output[3,4,5,5,4,null,7]

3#1650Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree IIIMedium

You are given two nodes p and q of a binary tree in which EVERY node also has a pointer to its parent. Return their lowest common ancestor: the lowest node that has both p and q below it (a node counts as below itself). Example: in the tree [3,5,1,6,2,0,8,null,null,7,4] with p = 5 and q = 1 → 3. (A tree written as a list reads level by level, top to bottom and left to right; null means there is no node in that spot.)

Example inputtree [3,5,1,6,2,0,8,null,null,7,4], p=5, q=1
→
Output3

Why? Each tree node knows its parent. Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes.

💡 Key idea Walk two pointers up the parent links; when one reaches the top, restart it at the other node. They meet exactly at the common ancestor after equal total steps.

Edge / failure case p=5, q=4 → 5
Node 4 is below node 5, so 5 is itself the lowest common ancestor.

There are hens and grains on a line (positions given as numbers). A hen eats a grain when they are at the same position (instantly); one hen can eat many grains. 3#164Maximum GapMedium

Given a list of numbers nums, imagine sorting it; return the largest difference between two NEIGHBOURING numbers in the sorted order (0 if the list has fewer than 2 numbers). Try to do it in linear time. Example: [3,6,9,1] → sorted 1,3,6,9 → the biggest gap is 3 → 3.

Example input[3, 6, 9, 1]
→
Output3

Why? After sorting, what is the biggest difference between neighbouring numbers? Do it without a full sort.

💡 Key idea With n numbers the biggest gap is at least (max−min)/(n−1). Drop numbers into buckets of that width, keeping only each bucket's min and max; the answer is the largest gap between one bucket's max and the next non-empty bucket's min.

A single number has no neighbours, so the gap is 0.

14#2039The Time When the Network Becomes IdleMedium

A network has n servers (0 is the master) connected by two-way wires. Example inputedges [[0,1],[1,2]], patience [0,2,1]
→
Output8

💡 Key idea BFS gives each server's distance d to the master; the round trip is 2d. A server resends at multiples of patience while < 2d, so its last message is sent at ((2d − 1) // patience) · patience and the reply arrives 2d later. The network is idle one second after the latest reply.

Edge / failure case patience 10 → 3
Both servers are 1 step from the master with huge patience, so there are no resends: the last reply arrives at 2, idle at 3.

Why? In a weighted graph, an edge is 'critical' if removing it makes the minimum spanning tree (MST) heavier (or impossible); 'pseudo-critical' if it appears in some MST but not all. List both kinds (by edge index).

💡 Key idea Compute the MST weight W. For each edge: Kruskal without it — if the weight rises (or the graph disconnects) it is critical. Otherwise Kruskal with it forced in — if the weight is still W it is pseudo-critical.

Edge / failure case a square → [[], [0, 1, 2, 3]]
All edges have equal weight: none is critical, all are pseudo-critical.

Cities are labelled 1…n. Cities x and y are directly connected if they have a common divisor strictly greater than the threshold. For each query [a, b] say whether the cities are connected (directly or through a chain of cities). Example: n=6, threshold=2, queries [[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]] → [False, False, True].

Example inputn=6, threshold=2, queries [[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]]
→
Output[False, False, True]

Why? Cities 1…n; two cities are directly connected if they share a divisor larger than the threshold. Answer queries: are cities a and b connected (directly or through other cities)?

💡 Key idea Instead of testing pairs, for every number z > threshold union all its multiples (z, 2z, 3z, …): they all share the divisor z. Then answer each query by comparing roots.

Edge / failure case threshold 0 → [True, True, True, True, True]
Threshold 0: any two numbers sharing a divisor (≥1) are connected, so all are.

131#1697Checking Existence of Edge Length Limited PathsHard

A graph with n nodes has weighted edges (several edges between the same pair are allowed). For each query [p, q, limit] decide whether a path from p to q exists whose every edge is STRICTLY shorter than the limit. Example: n=3, edges [[0,1,2],[1,2,4],[2,0,8],[1,0,16]], queries [[0,1,2],[0,2,5]] → [false, true].

Example inputn=3, edges=[[0,1,2],[1,2,4],[2,0,8],[1,0,16]], queries=[[0,1,2],[0,2,5]]
→
Output[false, true]

Why? Query (0,1,limit 2): the only 0–1 edge has length 2, which is not below 2 → false. Query (0,2,limit 5): 0–1 (2) and 1–2 (4) are both below 5 → true.

💡 Key idea Sort edges by length and queries by limit. Walk the queries in increasing limit order and union every edge shorter than that limit before answering — then 'is there a path' is just 'are they in the same group'.

Edge / failure case strict limit → [True, False]
With limit 14 all edges work; with limit 13 the edge of length 13 is too long.

Process the friend requests in order: a request is approved if it does not break any restriction; approved requests make them friends. Return a list of true/false per request. Example inputn=3, restrictions=[[0,1]], requests=[[0,2],[2,1]]
→

Why? Request 0–2 is fine. Request 2–1 would put 0 and 1 in the same friend group, which is forbidden, so it is rejected.

💡 Key idea Keep friend groups with Union Find. For a request, look at the two groups; if any restricted pair would end up with one person in each group, reject it. Otherwise merge.

Edge / failure case several restrictions → [True, False, True, False]
1–2 is itself a restricted pair → rejected; 3–1 is fine; 3–4 would put 0 and 1 in one group → rejected.
